title: Seva of the purse
hookLine: many Sikhs set aside a tenth of what they earn for the common good

lines: PAYDAY, AND IT'S ALL SPOKEN FOR.
cards: A hundred days. Take a second with that. Now, payday.
The money lands, and within an hour most of it has somewhere to be. Rent. The phone bill.
Groceries. That thing you've been waiting to buy. By the time you think about giving, it's whatever's left, which usually isn't much.
Now flip it. The money lands, and before the rent, before anything, one small slice is set aside. Not for you.

teach.h: DAS AND VANDH: A TENTH SHARE.
teach.b: Daswandh. Das is ten. Vandh, a share, a portion.
A tenth share. It's the seva of the purse, dhan seva, the third of tan, man and dhan.
Many Sikhs set aside a tenth of what they earn for the common good: the gurdwara, the langar, schools, disaster relief, a neighbor in trouble.

teach.h: BUILDING AMRITSAR, A TENTH AT A TIME.
teach.b: Tradition says the practice took shape in the time of the fourth and fifth Gurus, when Sikhs were asked to give a tenth, and those gifts helped build the city of Amritsar and the Harmandir Sahib you met on day sixty.
You first met the tenth on day thirteen, inside the second pillar, share what you earn.

Today, the part that day left out: who carried the money. Sikhs lived far from the Guru, so tradition says agents called masands were appointed to collect the offerings and bring them in. For a while it worked.
Then, tradition says, some masands kept what they collected and lorded it over the givers. Guru Gobind Singh ended the masand system and asked Sikhs to bring their offerings to the Guru directly.
So daswandh has two halves: give honestly, and make sure what's given is handled honestly.
Many Sikhs still ask where their tenth goes: a gurdwara committee with open accounts, a langar, a school, a relief fund they trust. A tenth isn't a law you're fined for missing.
Sikhs treat it as a discipline and an ideal. Some give more. People with very little give time instead.
And many Sikhs say the money came from the Giver in the first place, so daswandh just passes some of it on.

how: Many Sikhs set aside daswandh, a tenth of their earnings, for the gurdwara, the langar, education and relief work; others give their time in its place.

o: a tenth of what you earn, set aside for others
a yearly fee every Sikh pays to the gurdwara
a gift of food brought to the gurdwara on holidays

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: daswandh is a fine Sikhs must pay
it's a discipline and an ideal, not a fine. some give more, and some give time instead.
das is ten, vandh is a share.
Guru Gobind Singh ended the masand system
tradition says some masands kept the offerings, so he asked Sikhs to bring them to the Guru directly.

games.q: payday. the money has landed, and the bills are waiting. when does daswandh suggest you set the tenth aside?
o: once a year, if there's anything spare.
games.why: many Sikhs set the tenth aside first. they say the money came from the Giver anyway; daswandh passes some of it on.

practice: Think of what comes in for you in a week or a month, a paycheck, an allowance, and find a tenth of it in your head; no exact number needed.

Hold that number and notice how it feels, small, huge, scary or easy; there's no right answer. Then picture it going somewhere good, one real place or person; you're not committing to anything, just looking.

wordCard.voice: Daswandh. A tenth share: the part of what you earn that many Sikhs set aside for others, first.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: a tenth share, set aside for others.

carryVoice: Your line: a tenth, for others. Set aside first, not from what's left. A hundred days, and counting.
